questions.question: What probability reversal defines the prosecutor's fallacy?
options: Treating $\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)$ as if it were $\mathbb{P}(E)$
Treating $\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)$ as if it were $\mathbb{P}(H\mid E)$
Treating $\mathbb{P}(E\cap H)$ as if it were $\mathbb{P}(E)\mathbb{P}(H)$
Treating $\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)$ as if it were $1-\mathbb{P}(E\mid H^c)$

questions.question: A DNA profile occurs in one person in a million. Which statement commits the prosecutor's fallacy?
options: An innocent match has probability $10^{-6}$, so a guilty person matches with probability $1-10^{-6}$
Among $10^7$ possible sources, about $10$ innocent people would also match
An innocent match has probability $10^{-6}$, so the suspect is innocent with probability $10^{-6}$
About $10$ people match, so the DNA evidence is irrelevant

questions.question: Why can rare evidence fail to be decisive?
options: Rare evidence lowers the prior probability of the hypothesis
Bayes' rule uses only $P(E\mid H)$, ignoring alternative explanations
Its probability $P(E\mid H)$ is the same as $P(H\mid E)$
It may occur under competing hypotheses or small priors

questions.question: How does prevalence matter in medical-test reasoning?
options: Prior disease probability, affecting the posterior.
It is irrelevant once sensitivity is high.
It is the same as the false-positive rate
It makes all tests independent

questions.question: A suspicious transaction pattern occurs in $1\%$ of legitimate transactions. Why is this not enough to conclude fraud?
options: We also need the fraud base rate and the pattern probability under fraud
The pattern is not an event
Conditional probabilities are always equal
The $1\%$ figure is already the probability of fraud given the observed pattern

questions.question: A suspect is drawn uniformly from $10^6$ people, exactly one of whom is the culprit. The culprit matches the crime-scene DNA for sure; an innocent person matches with probability $10^{-5}$. The suspect matches. Approximately what is the probability that the suspect is innocent?
options: About $0.91$
About $0.09$

questions.question: Let $E$ and $H$ be events with $\mathbb{P}(E\cap H)>0$. Under which condition does swapping the conditional give the right number, that is, $\mathbb{P}(H\mid E)=\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)$?
options: Exactly when $E$ and $H$ are independent
Exactly when $\mathbb{P}(E)=\mathbb{P}(H)$
Exactly when $\mathbb{P}(H)=\tfrac{1}{2}$
Exactly when $\mathbb{P}(E\mid H^c)=0$
